# Clusterbuck

> A LAN-first LLM broker for client applications. It provides an OpenAI-compatible
> synchronous endpoint for interactive work and a durable HTTP job queue for work
> that may wait for an available or sleeping worker.

## Client integration

- [README](README.md): deployment overview, the two execution paths, and reachability rules.
- [Protocol contract](docs/protocols.md): authoritative prose contract for every request, response, state, and retry rule.
- [System design](docs/design.md): routing, privacy, capability scoring, waking, and cloud-fallback design.
- [JSON schemas](contract/): machine-readable contracts for async jobs, worker results and errors.
- [Reference client](examples/client/cbk_client.py): the durable-job lifecycle written out once — idempotent submit, persist, poll, fresh-key rerun, cancel — run by the end-to-end suite.

## Connection and authentication

Set the coordinator's base URL, for example `http://coordinator.lan:8018`.
All API routes except documented health/static/bootstrap/worker routes require the
operator key when `CBK_API_KEY` is configured. Send either:

```http
X-CBK-Api-Key: <key>
```

or `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Treat this as an operator credential: it is
authentication, not per-client authorisation. Do not put it in a URL.

## Choose an execution path

The two paths are addressed differently. Sync **targets a ready capability**: you name an
alias, and it binds that deployment as it stands now. Async **declares an intended
outcome**: you describe the need (`task_class`, `min_ability`, `requires`) and Clusterbuck
chooses, waits and wakes. Pick the path by whether a person is waiting, not by what the
work is. Keep product context — why you are asking, how the answer should be framed — in
`messages`; Clusterbuck routes on intent and requirements and never reads it.

Use the synchronous path only when a person is waiting and a reachable model server
is expected to answer immediately. It is OpenAI Chat Completions compatible:

```http
POST /v1/chat/completions
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "model": "8b-extract",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this text."}],
  "temperature": 0.2,
  "max_tokens": 500
}
```

The `model` is a Clusterbuck capability alias, not necessarily the underlying model
name, and it binds whatever deployment backs that alias now — it names a target, not a
need. Discover registered aliases with `GET /v1/models`, or `GET /fleet` for each alias's
configured model, `cloud` flag, `description`, `cloud_fallback` (the provider account the
tier falls back to when it cannot be served, `null` for none), and two things a sync
client needs to choose one:

- `features` — what the model is declared able to do (`json_schema`, `tools`, `vision`,
  `context_tokens`; `null` means undeclared). Sync does not apply `requires`, so pick an
  alias that declares what you need — e.g. `json_schema` for structured output — and
  still validate what comes back.
- `health` — whether the coordinator can reach that alias's model server:
  `{state, checked_at, last_ok_at, last_error}`, `state` one of `ready`, `degraded`,
  `unreachable`, `unknown`. It is refreshed every `CBK_MODEL_PROBE_S` (30s by default),
  so treat it as recent, not live. A request is never refused on it.

A successful response is a normal OpenAI-style chat completion. A failed call is not
retried for you, and its error carries a stable `code` (see *Errors* below):
`capability_not_found` (404) for an alias that does not exist, `model_server_unreachable`,
`model_server_timeout` or `model_server_error` when the alias exists but its model server
failed, `fleet_not_configured` (503) when there is no fleet, and `cloud_budget_exhausted`
(422) when the alias is a cloud tier and the monthly cloud budget is spent. A sync failure does not mean
the async worker route is unavailable: an unreachable-server error carries
`use_async: true` when something is consuming that capability's queue or a machine
serving it can be woken, so `POST /jobs` is worth trying.

The sync path forwards straight to a capability's model server: it does not route by
ability, apply `requires`, or wake a sleeping machine. Anything that needs those goes
through `POST /jobs`. It is metered (token counts and cost, never text) and held to the
cloud budget. If the operator gave a tier a cloud fallback, a failed call to that tier's
model server may be answered by a hosted provider instead. The sync request has no
`privacy` field, so that is operator policy, not the client's choice. Once the budget is
spent, no sync call reaches a provider.

Use the asynchronous path for batch work, long-running work, or requests that may
wait for capacity. It is the correct route when a sleeping worker may be woken or a
job should survive a client disconnect.

```http
POST /jobs
Idempotency-Key: <new-opaque-key-for-this-logical-call>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "task_class": "summarize",
  "min_ability": 6,
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this text."}],
  "params": {"temperature": 0.2, "max_tokens": 500},
  "urgency": "waitable",
  "privacy": "local_only",
  "deadline": "2026-09-23T12:00:00Z",
  "requires": {"context_tokens": 32768},
  "submitter": {"app": "my-client", "request_id": "req_123"}
}
```

The asynchronous request must use exactly one addressing method:

- Preferred: `task_class` plus `min_ability` (1-10), so Clusterbuck selects a measured,
  sufficiently capable artifact. Task classes are `extract`, `summarize`, `reason` and
  `code`.
- Advanced: `capability`, such as `8b-extract` or `30b-reason`, to select a
  supply-side tier directly.

Send either `messages` (OpenAI-style, roles `system` / `user` / `assistant`) or a
`prompt` string. A single content string is capped at 1 MiB and `messages` at 512
entries; larger requests are rejected with `422`.

`privacy` defaults to `local_only`; that setting never allows cloud routing. Set
`cloud_ok` only when the data and budget policy allow a hosted provider. Use `urgent`,
`necessary`, or `waitable` for `urgency`. Give user-visible work a `deadline` and/or
`escalate_after_min`: a waitable job with neither may wait indefinitely.

## When a job goes to the cloud

Local first, always. A job reaches a hosted provider only if it is `cloud_ok`, the
monthly cloud budget allows it, and one of these holds:

- **No local artifact is good enough.** Need-shaped routing found nothing local that
  clears `min_ability` and `requires`, but a cloud artifact does.
- **The local tier cannot be served at submit.** Its urgency is `necessary` or `urgent`,
  no machine is reading the tier, and none can be woken. A need-shaped job goes to the
  cheapest cloud artifact that clears the same bar. A job addressed by `capability` goes
  to that tier's `cloud_fallback` (shown by `GET /fleet`), or waits if there is none.
- **Nothing came before the deadline.** The job was queued locally, still nothing is
  reading its tier, and its `deadline` is within the rescue window (120 s by default). It
  is moved to a cloud artifact chosen at submit against the same ability bar. A job with
  no `deadline` is not moved, unless the operator has enabled that.

A tier that is up but slow keeps its work: speed never sends a job to the cloud.
`waitable` jobs never use the cloud until escalation promotes them to `necessary`.

When a job ran in the cloud, `GET /jobs/{id}` shows it. `capability` names the cloud tier,
which may not be the one you sent (it changes on a submit-time fallback or a rescue), and
`worker` reads `cloud:<provider>`. Nothing else about the job changes: the same
`result`, `usage` and terminal statuses.

## Hard requirements: `requires`

`requires` states what the model must be able to do, separately from how well it does
it. It is a filter applied before ability is compared, and it works with both
addressing forms:

```json
"requires": {"context_tokens": 60000, "tools": true, "json_schema": true, "vision": true}
```

- Every field is optional. Only truthy values filter: `"vision": false` means "I don't
  need vision", not "exclude models that have it".
- `context_tokens` is declared by you. Clusterbuck does not estimate prompt size, so a
  client sending a large document must say how much context it needs, or risk it being
  routed to a model that silently truncates it.
- A model that does not declare a feature counts as not having it. If nothing qualifies,
  the submit fails with `422`, code `requirements_unsatisfied`, naming the model and the
  missing feature. That is a different fix from an ability miss (`ability_unsatisfied`):
  usually an operator catalog entry, not a better model.
- `requires.tools` only selects a model declared able to emit tool calls; `params.tools`
  is forwarded. A job is one completion: `tool_calls` come back in `result`, and nothing
  resumes the job. Run the tool yourself and submit a new job carrying its result. A
  tool-capable model is given no authority by Clusterbuck — you decide which calls to honour.
- For structured output, set both `requires.json_schema: true` and
  `params.response_format` (e.g. `{"type": "json_object"}`). Without the requirement,
  `response_format` is dropped on the async path, because routing has not checked the
  model can honour it. Validate the JSON you get back either way.

## Poll, persist, and cancel async work

`POST /jobs` returns `202` with `{ "id", "result_key", "status": "queued" }`.
Poll `GET /jobs/{id}` until `status` is terminal: `done`, `failed`, `expired`, or
`cancelled`. A completed job returns its OpenAI-style chat completion in `result`, with
token counts in `usage`. Any other terminal status carries a message in `error` and a
stable `error_code` to branch on: `job_expired`, `job_cancelled`, `job_orphaned` (resubmit
under a fresh key), `job_abandoned`, `capability_misconfigured`, `worker_failed`, or a
`model_server_*` code. Persist the result and the code immediately: both expire after
`CBK_RESULT_TTL_S` (24 hours by default).

All four terminal statuses are final. `done` and `failed` come from the first result
written, so a job reported `failed` will not later turn up `done`. `expired` and
`cancelled` are decided by the coordinator, and a result that arrives afterwards (from a
worker that had already claimed the job) is discarded. A queued job whose queue entry was
trimmed away is reported `failed` rather than left `queued` forever.

The poll response also carries `deadline`, `escalates_at` and `expires_at`.
`expires_at: null` means nothing will ever give up on the job: a `waitable` job with no
`deadline` and no `escalate_after_min` waits for a capable worker indefinitely, which on
a fleet that sleeps is by design.

`queue_position` counts only unclaimed jobs ahead of yours; `0` can still mean work is
in flight. `started_at` and `worker` are best-effort coordinator observations, so use
`status` as the primary state signal.

Use `DELETE /jobs/{id}` to stop waiting. `cancelled` guarantees the job never ran;
`cancelling` means a worker already held it, so its result will be discarded when it
finishes.

## Reliability rules

Use an `Idempotency-Key` on every `POST /jobs`: printable ASCII, at most 255
characters. Reuse the same key only when retrying the same logical submission after an
uncertain response. A replay returns `200` (not `202`) with `Idempotency-Replayed: true`
and the existing job's `id`, and enqueues nothing. A submit rejected with `400` or `422`
does not consume its key, so the same key can be retried once the fleet can serve it.
To run the work again after any terminal status, use a **fresh** key: a key has no TTL,
so the old one keeps returning the old, finished job.
`submitter.request_id` is diagnostic provenance only, not a deduplication key.

Branch on `error.code`, not on the HTTP status or the message (see *Errors*). Do not
retry a request whose error has `retryable: false` unchanged. For async work, retry
transport failures with the same idempotency key, then poll the returned job.

Never send prompts, completions, or credentials to Redis directly. Clients communicate
only with the coordinator HTTP API; workers pull queued jobs themselves.

## Errors

Every error is OpenAI's envelope, so the stock SDK exposes the code as `.code`:

```json
{"error": {"message": "…", "type": "invalid_request_error", "code": "capability_not_found",
           "retryable": false, "param": "model", "capability": "…"},
 "detail": "…"}
```

- `code` is the contract; the message is for people and may change. `detail` repeats the
  message for older clients and is deprecated.
- `retryable: true` means the identical request may succeed if retried soon (a transient
  model-server failure). It never means "retry until the fleet changes".
- HTTP codes in use: `invalid_request`, `unauthorized`, `not_found`,
  `fleet_not_configured`, `capability_not_found`, `capability_misconfigured`,
  `reservation_invalid`, `model_server_unreachable`, `model_server_timeout`,
  `model_server_error`, `model_request_rejected`. A refused `POST /jobs` is always `422`,
  told apart by code: `ability_unsatisfied`, `requirements_unsatisfied`,
  `capability_not_found`, `cloud_not_permitted`, `cloud_budget_exhausted`.
- A job's terminal state carries `error_code` beside `error` (see above). The full
  vocabulary, with meanings, is
  [contract/error-codes.json](contract/error-codes.json).
